title: India Posted a Surprise $7.1 Billion Surplus Last Quarter. The Diaspora Sent the Money.
excerpt: Remittances from Indians working abroad surged 28% to $43.5 billion in a single quarter — the largest jump in years — as Gulf-based workers transferred funds home amid the West Asia crisis.
body:
India recorded a surprise current account surplus of $7.1 billion in the January–March quarter of fiscal year 2025-26, the Reserve Bank of India disclosed on Monday. The number, equivalent to 0.7 per cent of GDP, confounded economists who had expected the deficit cycle to continue — and the biggest driver was something deeply personal to the Indian diaspora: remittances.

Personal transfer receipts — overwhelmingly money sent home by Indians working abroad — surged to $43.5 billion in the quarter, up from $33.9 billion a year ago. The 28 per cent jump is extraordinary even by India's standards as the world's largest remittance recipient, and it coincides with the West Asia crisis that has upended the lives of millions of Gulf-based Indian workers.

"The positive surprise on the current account was due to remittances. The West Asia crisis may have resulted in precautionary transfer of funds," said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank. The reading suggests that Indian workers in the Gulf — facing the uncertainty of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, Hormuz disruptions, and rising living costs — are sending money home faster, either as a hedge against displacement or because a weaker rupee makes transfers more valuable in rupee terms.

The surplus marked a sharp reversal from the $13.2 billion current account deficit recorded in the October–December quarter. Net services receipts also contributed, rising to $60.4 billion from $53.3 billion a year earlier, powered by growth in computer services and business process exports — the bread and butter of India's IT sector.

But the headline surplus masks a deteriorating trade picture. The merchandise trade deficit widened to $83.4 billion in the quarter, up from $59.3 billion a year ago, driven by costlier oil imports and a weaker rupee inflating the import bill. For the full financial year 2025-26, India still ran a current account deficit of $25.2 billion, or 0.6 per cent of GDP — unchanged as a share of the economy from the previous year but higher in absolute terms.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the data sends a complicated signal. The surge in remittances is partly structural — India received $137.7 billion in worker remittances in calendar year 2024, according to the International Organisation for Migration, more than double what the second-largest recipient, Mexico, received. But the Q4 spike likely reflects fear as much as fundamentals.

Indians in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar — who collectively account for a significant share of global remittances to India — face an environment of rising costs, job uncertainty in oil-dependent economies, and travel advisories from the Ministry of External Affairs. The precautionary motive that economists are flagging could also mean that some of these workers are quietly preparing for repatriation.

The RBI, meanwhile, is trying to harness this diaspora lifeline more aggressively. On Friday, it announced a package of measures to attract more NRI deposits, including hedging benefits for banks raising three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits from non-resident Indians. State Bank of India estimates the measures could bring in more than $34 billion in fresh inflows.

For the full year, India's balance of payments recorded a deficit of $23.6 billion, underlining that while the quarterly surplus is welcome, the structural pressure from higher oil imports and record foreign portfolio outflows has not abated. The question now is whether the remittance surge will hold as the Gulf crisis evolves — or whether it was a one-quarter precautionary burst that will fade as uncertainty either resolves or, worse, normalises.
